prerequisites: A subject containing basic concepts of combustion

learning_outcomes.text: Have systematic knowledge and understanding of the key concepts and aspects of energy consumption in the transport sector, the main propulsion technologies involved, the fuels used, and their emissions.

Have adequate knowledge of the operation and energy efficiency of the main engines used for propulsion in road, rail, air, and maritime transport, as well as emerging hybrid and electric propulsion technologies.

Be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate, and solve problems of thermal and energy characterization of main propulsion systems using established methods in thermodynamics and fluid mechanics.
Be able to choose and apply relevant analytical and modeling methods in thermal and fluid engineering for the characterization of thermodynamic cycles of propulsion engines.
Be able to conduct bibliographic searches, use databases, and other sources of information.
Be able to select and use appropriate equipment, tools, and methods to empirically evaluate the different energy consumptions and losses in land, air, and maritime transport.
Be able to combine theory and practice to solve problems of characterizing the energy efficiency of a given vehicle's propulsion system along with its losses and polluting emissions.
Function effectively both individually and as part of a team.
Demonstrate awareness of the responsibility of engineering practice, its social and environmental impact, and commitment to professional ethics, responsibility, and standards of engineering practice.
A systematic understanding of the key concepts and aspects of their engineering branch.
An adequate knowledge of their engineering branch, including some knowledge at the forefront of their field.
The ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate, and solve engineering problems using established methods.
The ability to choose and apply relevant analytical and modeling methods.
The ability to conduct bibliographic searches, use databases, and other sources of information.
The ability to select and use appropriate equipment, tools, and methods.
The ability to combine theory and practice to solve engineering problems.
Function effectively both individually and as part of a team.
Demonstrate awareness of the responsibility of engineering practice, its social and environmental impact, and commitment to professional ethics, responsibility, and standards of engineering practice.

Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is usually found at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects that involve knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional way and possess the competencies that are usually demonstrated by elaborating and defending arguments and solving problems within their field of study.
Knowledge and ability to analyze and assess the social and environmental impact of technical solutions, and to apply environmental and sustainability technologies.
Knowledge and ability to apply computational and experimental tools for the analysis and quantification of mechanical engineering problems.
Applied knowledge of thermal engineering.
Applied knowledge of the fundamentals of fluid-mechanical systems and machines.

syllabus_topics: Introduction: Energy consumption in transport vs. world consumption.
Transport sectors: means of transport (people vs. goods).
Types of propulsion plants: thermal engines and electric motors. Reciprocating engines, gas turbines, electric motors, and other systems.
Types of liquid and gaseous fuels and their uses in transport. Biofuels. Other forms of energy storage.
Pollutants and impact. Direct and indirect contamination. Atmospheric pollutants CO2, NOx, SOx, HC, CO, particles and comparison of emissions by sector.

Reciprocating engines in transport: Architecture and processes in reciprocating engines. Two-stroke and four-stroke engines. Compression-ignition engines (diesel), spark-ignition engines (gasoline and gas).
Power, torque, efficiency, and specific consumption.
Full-load characteristic curves.
Combustion, emission, control, and mitigation of pollutants in reciprocating engines.
Gas turbines in transport: Architecture and processes in gas turbines.
Brayton cycles for power generation.
Gas cycle in turbojet without and with afterburner. Gas cycle in turbofan.
Efficiencies and performance.
Combustion, emission, and mitigation of pollutants in gas turbines.
Electric propulsion in transport: 100% electric vehicles.
Hybrid vehicles.
Energy storage systems: batteries.
Propulsion efficiencies in transport: Drag forces and propulsive power.
Efficiencies in land, air, and maritime transport.
Auxiliary systems in transport: Energy consumption in auxiliary systems.
Cooling systems, air conditioning, cabin pressurization, electrical and electronic systems. Other auxiliary systems.
Control and management of transport systems: Transport control and management.
Road, rail, air, and maritime traffic. International transport modes.
teaching_methods: Laboratory sessions (calculations with measurement/model results, report writing)
Individual or group student work (solving exercises, report writing)

assessment_methods.method: Continuous assessment (Class participation, individual problem solving, group work, partial exam, lab practices)

assessment_rules: To pass the subject, two requirements must be met: the final exam grade must be equal to or greater than 2.0 out of 10, and the overall grade for the subject must be equal to or greater than 5.0 out of 10. Continuous assessment is based on class participation, individual problem solving, group assignments, a partial exam, and laboratory practices.
